item.title: 🔴 F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic.

item.title: 🔵 Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

item.title: 🔴 A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.

item.title: 🔴 European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems.

The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.”

item.description:
Why this matters: Authentication bypass — review access controls and look for unauthorized access.

Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching.

Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5.

item.title: 🔴 Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work.

For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level.

But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach.

The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done.

item.title: 🔴 AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both a…

item.title: 🔴 A new critical Java hole illustrates the enterprise IT visibility problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

When cybersecurity research firm Calif published details Tuesday of a potentially major Java security flaw, dubbed Java4Shell, it described an unauthenticated attacker’s ability to read Java heap memory, steal private keys, tokens, and session secrets, and reach remote code execution (RCE).

With Java being all-but-ubiquitous in today’s enterprise, coupled with the inability of CISOs to have visibility into every instance of it in their estate, this means that the bug could be a big problem for IT.

Java, which has had its fair share of cybersecurity issues lately, is well-known for safely handling memory. That is why a Java bug affecting memory management is so dangerous. item.title: 🔴 Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.

item.title: 🟠 The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality.

Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing.

item.description:

The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts.

The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure.

“He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit. “We’re EU based.”

When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.”

The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.”

item.title: 🟠 Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

item.title: 🔴 Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. 

Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC.

Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack.

“Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI,…

item.title: 🟠 Google and Anthropic push for faster patches as AI collapses bug discovery timelines
item.description:
Why this matters: Endpoint-security changes may affect detection and alerting.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline.

Project Zero is Google’s elite vulnerability research team that regularly reports vulnerabilities in widely used open-source and proprietary software, much of which is critical to internet infrastructure. Its 90-day deadline for vendors to produce patches before the team releases vulnerability details publicly was a major stake in the ground for the security research community when it was announced in 2014, and it has become the de facto standard for coordinated disclosure.

item.title: 🟠 California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
item.description:

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models.

The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. item.title: 🟠 Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors.

The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials.

item.title: 🔵 The benign true positive: When trusted AI agents look like attackers
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A coding agent opens hundreds of files, launches command-line tools and connects to an internal service to complete a task. A support agent authenticates to several systems, retrieves customer records and updates another application. A workflow agent enumerates cloud resources in seconds, then moves to the next stage of its assignment.

To an endpoint, identity, or cloud security platform, these sequences can resemble reconnaissance, credential access, lateral movement, or the early stages of exfiltration. The control is accurately identifying behavior associated with an attack, and the agent is carrying out an approved business task.

item.title: 🔴 Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

item.title: 🔵 Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

item.title: 🔵 Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

Source: Krebs on Security  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: 17d
